opus-5.5.text:
I think what strikes me most about Kaiming is his taste — his ability to see what really matters in a problem and strip away everything else. A lot of people, when they do research, tend to pile things on. They add modules, add tricks, add complexity, because complexity looks like effort and it's easier to justify a paper that way. Kaiming goes in the opposite direction. If you look at ResNet, the core idea is almost embarrassingly simple: just add an identity shortcut. But that simplicity came from a very deep understanding of why deep networks were failing to train. It wasn't simple because it was easy; it was simple because he had thought it through so carefully that only the essential part remained.

When I was working with him, I noticed he has this habit of asking, "What is the minimal thing we need to show this works?" And he's extremely rigorous about experiments. He wants every claim to be backed by a clean ablation, and he's not satisfied until the result is something he really believes, not just something that beats a number on a leaderboard. He would rather spend extra months making sure an idea is solid than rush something out.

Another thing is that he cares a lot about generality. He's not interested in a trick that gives you half a point on one benchmark. He wants methods that people across the field can pick up and use, things that become part of the basic toolkit. ResNet, Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, MoCo, MAE — they all have this flavor. They're clean, they're general, and they kind of open up a direction rather than close one.

And personally, he's very calm and humble. He doesn't chase hype. He's willing to work on things that are unfashionable if he thinks they're important. For me, that was a big lesson — that good research is really about clarity of thinking and patience, and that the most impactful work often looks obvious only in hindsight.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that strikes me most about Kaiming is how ruthlessly simple he is willing to be. A lot of us, when we have an idea, our instinct is to add things. More components, more tricks, more moving parts, because that feels like progress and it is easier to get a few points on a benchmark that way. Kaiming goes the other direction. He keeps asking, what is the minimal thing here? What can I remove and still have it work? ResNet is the obvious example. The residual connection is almost embarrassingly simple when you see it, but the reason it has lasted more than a decade is precisely that simplicity. There is nothing to break.

The second thing is his patience with the problem itself. When we worked together, I noticed he would sit with a question for a very long time before touching code. He wanted to understand why something fails, not just that it fails. When we did ConvNeXt, the whole project was really an exercise in that mindset. Everyone had decided transformers were winning because of attention, and he kept pushing on whether that was actually the reason or whether it was a pile of training and design details nobody had bothered to port back. That kind of skepticism toward the consensus explanation, combined with the discipline to test it one variable at a time, is rare.

And honestly, the third thing is taste in what to work on. He does not chase whatever is hot that month. He picks problems where, if the answer is clean, it will still matter in five years. MAE is like that too. It was not the first masked pretraining idea for vision, but he found the version where the whole thing reduces to one or two decisions that really matter, and then he showed it with almost no decoration. I try to hold myself to that standard, and I fail at it constantly, which tells you how hard it actually is.

astra-6.text:
What impresses me most is his ability to get to the core of a problem. A lot of research involves adding things—another module, another loss, another trick. His approach often seems to go in the opposite direction: What is actually necessary? Can we make the idea simpler and still solve the fundamental problem?

And that kind of simplicity is hard-earned. When you see the final result, it can feel obvious, but identifying the right question and making the evidence really convincing takes tremendous care. That combination of conceptual clarity and rigor is what I find especially impressive.

sol-6.1.text:
What really impresses me is his ability to identify the essential question and stay focused on it. It’s easy in research to add complexity—to add another module or another trick. The harder thing is to step back and ask, “Why do we need this? Can we make it simpler?”

And simplicity takes a lot of work. You have to understand the problem deeply, question your assumptions, and run careful experiments. That combination of clear thinking and patience is what I find especially impressive about Kaiming’s approach.
